cells.tense: There is a room in you where nothing has been chosen yet
cells.act: pick the one you would be sorriest to lose
cells.ask: Single out what you'd grieve to lose most, and keep that to yourself. Give it the first of whatever you have to give before anything else gets a share. Make wanting it the first decision you settle on.
cells.core:
You can be in the place before the choice, and something in you doesn't rush to close the door. You meet what's here as it is, without reaching for what it could become, and that's not naivety — it's the part of you that stays open because nothing is pressing it shut. Whatever's growing nearby gets to stay early for as long as it needs. You make the room before anyone has to explain the plant.

Among everything you're holding open, one thing matters to you more than the rest. Set your days by it. Give that one the first water — not the whole plan, just the first of it — and make wanting it the first decision you settle on about anything. A good deal of what's left will sit there unresolved, longer than feels comfortable. That's what choosing costs, and choosing is how the possibility finds out what it was.

cells.tense: By next week it will still be true that nothing has landed
cells.act: let what you are show without dimming it
cells.ask: Give a thing you're holding in the air a fixed shape — badly is fine. Your own hands, your own way, nobody told why. Let it be what it actually is.
cells.core:
Nothing has landed yet, and the not-landing is the thing you're guarding. Everything you're holding stays possible because it hasn't been made yet — next month it could still turn out to be anything, and nothing hardens into a thing that has to be answered for. It feels like keeping every door open. From where the possibilities sit, it looks like none of them is being allowed to find out what it is.

Open has a second half: a thing that already exists, allowed to stay that way long enough to grow as itself. Not forever — a week. Give something you're keeping possible a fixed shape, do it with your own hands, in your own way, and explain it to no one. What you pick stops being potential and becomes a single thing that happened. That's the light. It was already yours; doing it is how you find out.
cells.sheetLine: You're keeping it possible instead of letting it become.
cells.verb: Standing before anything is chosen yet
cells.place: The place where everything is still possible

cells.tense: The opening has been closed so long it no longer looks like a door
cells.act: look at the same thing longer, until it shows you more
cells.ask: Take one thing within reach — a chair, a window, a plant — and stay past your first glance. Wait until it offers a detail you didn't have. One is enough.
cells.core:
The place before the choice is still in you, but it isn't being entered. What's here arrives already settled — you read the first thing and move on, and what it might turn into doesn't get asked. You take things in, steadily. The room that happens in has gotten small.

Stay longer. Pick something within reach — a chair, a window, a plant — and hold your attention there beyond your usual turning away, until it offers something you hadn't noticed. Keep a count of what it offers: three, five, one. The count is the point, and it goes nowhere — you carry it to the next look. Possibility comes back through the eyes before it comes back through the hands.

cells.tense: The pen is down in a room where the writing is already happening
cells.act: picture it a year on, turned out well, and keep the picture
cells.ask: Take something you're already living — a job, a room, a regular walk — and picture it a year from now, going well. No plan, no telling. Keep the picture for as long as it keeps itself.
cells.core:
You're opening doors as you go — a route, a pause, a sentence that lands well — and ask why you did it and the answer is that you were simply following along. The choices are being made and they're decent ones; what's missing is your name on them. You file it under circumstance. The rooms you end up in don't.

Go back to wanting, with no plan attached. Take something you're already living — the job you go to, the room you sleep in, the walk you take most days — and picture it a year on, turned out well. Keep the picture for as long as it keeps itself, and don't turn it into a plan. Your hand is already in how it's going. Seeing it is how you get to know your hand was there.
